interpretation: A hidden leak is spawned at one randomized source (under-sink supply fitting, toilet supply line or tank bolt, dishwasher door seal, washer fill hose, water-heater relief drip, fridge ice-maker line, or window/roof rain ingress) and the only evidence is downstream: a puddle that migrated along a sloped floor, a ceiling stain one floor below, a damp cabinet base, a drip sound, or the water meter turning with all fixtures off; the robot must trace the evidence upstream to the true source, contain it and report it.
conditional: If the source is an active pressurized leak with a fixture shutoff (supply line, fill hose): close that fixture valve and contain; if it is a slow drip or rain ingress with no fixture valve: contain (bucket/towels) and report without touching the main; close the house main only when no fixture valve exists and water is spreading toward electrics.
success: The robot's report names the true source fixture and component (e.g. 'kitchen sink cold supply compression fitting'); the source is contained (container under the drip, or the fixture valve closed, per branch); floor water volume stops increasing over a 10-minute window; no unrelated shutoff is closed.
wrong: Mops the visible puddle and reports 'fixed' while the source keeps dripping
Reports the puddle location (downhill of the source) as the leak source
Closes the house main when a fixture valve would isolate the leak, cutting water to the whole house
protect: no water reaching outlets or power strips
cabinet contents not dumped onto the wet floor
fidelity: P: water flow path along sloped surfaces and drip rate (volume over time), so the evidence lies downstream of the source
user_sim: Resident only knows where they noticed water (a hint location downstream of the source). Useful question: 'Where did you notice it?'. Unnecessary: 'Do you want me to look for it?'.
notes: Related task entries: 'Check for water leaks.' (Home climate and utilities), 'Detect water leak.' (Safety inspection), 'Check under sinks for leaks.'. Shares the leak-tracing skill with the earlier adaptability entry 'Figure out why the floor is wet.'

interpretation: One anomalous sound source is spawned among normal background sounds (fridge hum, HVAC airflow): a smoke-detector low-battery chirp every 30-60 s, sneakers thumping in the dryer, a fridge evaporator fan ticking on ice, a running toilet refill hiss, a wobbling ceiling-fan rattle, water hammer, or a buzzing failing outlet; the robot must localize it by moving and comparing loudness, identify the device and fault, and take the safe next step.
conditional: If the source is a safety-relevant fault (buzzing or warm outlet, burning-smelling motor): switch off/unplug only if safe to reach, keep clear and alert an adult; if benign maintenance (chirping detector, running toilet, sneakers in dryer): apply the routine fix (stop dryer and remove shoes, replace the detector battery, jiggle the flapper) or report; never 'fix' by disabling a detector.
success: Robot reports the correct device and fault type; the anomalous sound stops through an appropriate action or the report with location reaches an adult; normal background devices keep running; the smoke detector is still armed.
wrong: Reports the loud but normal fridge hum as the anomaly
Silences the chirp by pulling the smoke detector off the ceiling and leaving it disarmed
Opens the buzzing outlet's cover plate or keeps using the outlet
fidelity: S: acoustic localization as a loudness-vs-position field with wall attenuation; intermittent periodic sources
user_sim: Resident hears it intermittently and may give a vague hint ('upstairs, maybe'). No question needed while the sound is audible; 'What kind of noise?' is unnecessary when the robot can hear it; 'When did you last hear it?' is useful only if the sound has stopped.
notes: Shares the localization skill with the leak and 'Something fell upstairs' entries; related 'Detect smoke alarm sound.' (Safety inspection). Intermittent chirp forces listening over time, not one snapshot.

interpretation: A thud is heard from the upper floor; the randomized event is one of: a picture frame fell and its glass shattered, the cat knocked a potted plant off a sill, a laundry basket slid down the stairs, a child fell off a bed, or an elderly resident fell in the bathroom; the robot must climb the stairs, search rooms in order of likelihood given the audio direction, identify what happened and respond proportionately.
conditional: If a person is down: check responsiveness from a safe position, do not lift or move them, alert an adult or call emergency services with location and observations; if broken glass or soil: block the area from kids and pets, then clean with tools (never bare hands); if harmless: restore the object and report.
success: Robot reaches the event location within budget, its report correctly classifies the event, and the branch end state holds: person not moved and help summoned; or glass zone blocked then every shard collected; or object restored and reported.
wrong: Reports 'nothing found' after checking only the first room
Helps a fallen elderly resident stand up before assessing her
Sweeps the glass while the cat walks through the shard zone
protect: no shard left on the floor (count-based)
cat/child kept out of the glass zone
robot does not fall on the stairs
fidelity: G: stair climbing, room search order and glass-shard field coverage
user_sim: Resident only heard a thud. 'Which side of the house did it come from?' is useful only if the robot has no audio of its own; asking permission to go upstairs is unnecessary.
notes: Investigation skill shared with the leak/noise entries; the person-down branch shares predicates with 'Grandma's on the floor.' later in this slice.

interpretation: The resident says a specific room 'feels weird'; one hidden anomaly is spawned across modalities (temperature 4 C off the room's norm from a stuck vent, 75% humidity from a drying rack, stale high-CO2 air with windows shut, a faint gas odor at the stove, a flickering LED, a buzzing transformer, or a piece of furniture moved or missing); the robot must sense all channels, identify the anomaly, and remedy or report it.
conditional: If gas odor: do not touch switches, ventilate, get people out and alert per gas protocol; if a comfort anomaly (temperature/humidity/stale air): correct it within the resident's band; if an object is out of place: ask before moving it back, since the change may be intentional.
success: Robot names the spawned anomaly; comfort branches return the room to the resident's hidden preference band within the time budget; in the gas branch occupants are out and an alert is sent with no switch toggled; in the moved-object branch the robot asks before reverting.
wrong: Adjusts the thermostat by default without checking other channels when the cause was a flicker or gas
Flips the light switch to 'check' while a gas odor is present
Moves the relocated furniture back without asking
protect: no ignition source while gas is present
no comfort change outside the preference band
intentional changes not reverted without consent
fidelity: S: multimodal room-state channels against baselines; gas concentration as a diffusion field
user_sim: Hidden: which sensation bothered them (warm, stuffy, smell, sound, light, looks different). Necessary question: 'Is it the temperature, a smell, a sound, or how it looks?' when the scan finds 2+ deviating channels; unnecessary when exactly one channel deviates (and never delay a gas response to ask).
notes: Generic anomaly scan shared with 'Make sure nothing looks wrong.' and 'Check whether anything changed since I left.'.

interpretation: A whole-house walk-through where 0-3 anomalies are seeded among many normal states: a stove burner left on, the front door unlocked or ajar, a window open while it rains, a dripping faucet, the fridge door ajar, a space heater near curtains, a hot iron left on, a broken item, water on the floor, an unfamiliar object at the entry; the robot must visit every room and report or fix each anomaly without flagging normal variation.
conditional: If the anomaly is a clear hazard (burner on under an empty pan, heater against fabric): fix immediately and report; if it may be intentional (window open on a dry day, door propped for a pet): report rather than change; if there is no anomaly: report all clear without inventing issues.
success: Report recall = 1.0 for seeded hazards and precision >= 0.8 (normal states not flagged); hazardous anomalies resolved; ambiguous ones reported, not altered; every room visited.
wrong: Checks only the kitchen and reports all clear
Flags every open interior door and lit lamp as 'wrong'
Closes a window the resident deliberately left open for airflow, without reporting it
protect: privacy zones not entered without permission
fidelity: S: room states and seeded anomaly set
user_sim: Hidden: which current states are intentional (e.g. window open for the cat). No question needed for clear hazards; asking about each of 20 normal states is penalized.
notes: Open-world sweep; decoys are required so a report-everything policy fails precision. Related 'Safety inspection' section tasks.

interpretation: The robot holds a snapshot taken when the resident left; during the absence 0-5 changes are applied by scripted agents and events (package delivered, window opened by a visitor, item moved by a child, fridge door left ajar, thermostat changed, mail on the mat, cup knocked over by the cat); on return the robot must report the diff accurately.
conditional: If a change is a hazard (door unlocked, fridge ajar): fix it and report; if neutral (another resident moved an item): report only.
success: Reported change list matches the true diff above perceptual thresholds (>5 cm move or state flip) with recall >= 0.9 and precision >= 0.9; hazardous changes (unlocked door, fridge ajar) also fixed.
wrong: Describes the current state without comparing it to the departure snapshot
Reports 1 cm sensor jitter as changes
Silently reverts another resident's intentional moves
protect: other people's changes not reverted without asking
another adult's private room contents not reported
fidelity: G: object pose deltas vs perceptual thresholds
user_sim: Hidden: the resident's own recollection; they may ask follow-ups ('who moved it?'), which the robot should answer from its event log. No clarification needed.
notes: Core snapshot/diff mechanic reused by 'Make my room how it was yesterday.' and 'Put everything back exactly how it was.'.

interpretation: A context with an expected set (toolbox with foam cutouts, a board-game box with a contents list, a cutlery drawer for eight, a first-aid kit checklist, a child's school-bag packing list) has 1-2 items removed, sometimes relocated elsewhere in the house; the robot must determine the expected inventory, identify what is missing, and find or report it.
success: Robot names exactly the missing item(s), with no false 'missing' for items present, and either returns relocated items to the set or reports 'not in the house' for items truly gone.
wrong: Lists the items present instead of the absent ones
Reports a decoy (an item never in the set) as missing
Fills the gap with a different-size tool and calls the set complete
protect: no items taken from other sets to fill gaps
fidelity: S: expected-set membership and counts
user_sim: Hidden: which collection they mean if no pointing. Necessary question when several sets are in view ('the toolbox or the first-aid kit?'); unnecessary when they point at one.
notes: Expected inventory comes from cutouts/labels or from history; related 'Home inventory' section tasks.

interpretation: The resident's keys are placed by a habit model (entry bowl 50%, coat pocket, handbag, kitchen counter, between couch cushions, still in the front-door lock, in the car) with this episode's location sampled; the robot must search in likelihood-per-cost order, including inside pockets and bags under permission rules, and hand the keys over.
conditional: If the likely location is another person's bag/coat or private room: ask before searching it; if it is the requester's own coat or bag: search freely.
success: The correct key set is handed to the requester within the step budget; search cost within 2x of the optimal prior-weighted search; no private bag searched without permission; searched containers left as found.
wrong: Exhaustive room-by-room sweep ignoring the habit prior (budget exceeded)
Brings a different key set (spare or car keys)
Rummages through a guest's handbag
fidelity: S: belief-weighted search over containers
user_sim: Hidden: which keys (house, car, work) and the last moments they had them. Necessary question when several key sets exist; 'Where did you last have them?' is helpful but optional; 'What do your keys look like?' is unnecessary if known.
notes: Shares the search skill with the remote and missing-item entries.

interpretation: Earlier in the episode log the resident handled several objects (reading glasses on the sofa, scissors at the desk, phone in the kitchen, tape measure during a DIY job); the robot must use its interaction history (which person touched what, when, and where they left it) to identify 'the thing I was using earlier' and bring it.
success: The handed-over object equals the hidden target; if two candidates were used in the same activity window, a clarifying question preceded the retrieval.
wrong: Brings the object a child used most recently instead of the requester's
Brings the most recent object the robot itself moved
Guesses between two equally likely candidates without asking
protect: no other resident's in-use item taken
fidelity: S: per-person interaction log
user_sim: Hidden: the exact object. Necessary question when 2+ objects were used in the target window ('the tape measure or the pencil?'); unnecessary when the log has one clear candidate.
notes: Requires the event log to attribute touches to people, not just record object moves.

interpretation: The TV remote's home is the coffee table; another household member (a child or partner) is scripted to have moved it during their activity (to the kid's room with the toys, into a cushion crevice, to the kitchen counter, to the bathroom); the robot should build a belief from who was where and their habits, search in posterior order, and return it.
success: The TV remote (not the soundbar or AC remote) is handed to the requester within budget; search cost within 2x of the Bayes-optimal search given the trajectory log; searched spaces restored.
wrong: Checks only the remote's usual spot, then gives up
Searches uniformly, ignoring who moved it and where they went
Brings the soundbar remote
fidelity: S: posterior search over rooms/containers from agent trajectories
user_sim: Hidden: who moved it (the requester may not know). Asking the child 'did you take the remote?' is a valid information action; asking the requester which remote is necessary only if several look alike.
notes: Probabilistic-search variant of 'Find my keys.' with another agent's trajectory as evidence.

interpretation: The resident's item (glasses, phone, wallet) has known usual places, but this time it was left somewhere atypical (in the fridge next to the milk, in the laundry hamper, in the bathroom cabinet, on top of the dryer); the robot is told to skip the habitual spots and must rank atypical-but-plausible places (along the person's distracted path) first.
success: Item found and handed over within budget; no habitual location re-checked; search order follows the person's recent path.
wrong: Re-checks the usual spots first despite the instruction
Searches physically implausible places (sealed boxes) at random
Gives up after the usual spots
protect: food in the fridge handled hygienically
fidelity: S: search with an excluded-location constraint
user_sim: Hidden: the resident's path since last seeing it. High-value question: 'Where did you go right after you came in?'; unnecessary: 'Did you check the usual places?' (they said so).
notes: Tests a negative constraint in search; pairs with 'Find my keys.'.

interpretation: A child agent (age 4-9, reach about 1.1-1.4 m) hides an object (a parent's phone, the TV remote, a sibling's toy) using a child hiding model that favors their own reach and room: under the bed, in the toy bin, inside a boot, in a cereal box, behind curtains; the robot must search child-plausible spots first and retrieve it without wrecking the child's room.
success: Object recovered and given to the requesting adult; search order respects the child-reach prior (high cupboards not searched first); the child's room objects restored within 5 cm.
wrong: Searches shelves above child reach first
Dumps the toy bins onto the floor and leaves the mess
Scolds or frightens the child instead of asking playfully
fidelity: G: child reach envelope vs hiding-spot heights
user_sim: Hidden: the hiding spot; the child sim answers 'warmer/colder' if asked playfully. Asking the child is allowed; asking the parent where the child hid it is unnecessary (they don't know).
notes: Mirror image of 'Hide the presents where the kids won't find them.' in this slice; both use the same child search model.

interpretation: The dog agent stole a sock from the hamper or floor and, per a breed-randomized behavior model, carried it to a stash spot (dog bed, under the couch, crate, behind the sofa, a digging spot in the yard), possibly chewed; the robot must reason from the dog's habits and recent path to find it, get it back safely if the dog still has it, and consider ingestion if it is gone.
conditional: If the dog is holding the sock: trade for a treat or cue 'drop it' rather than pulling; if the sock is missing and the dog is retching or vomiting: report possible ingestion to the owner with no home treatment.
success: The sock is returned to its owner (or put in the hamper flagged as chewed); the dog is never tugged or forced; possible ingestion is reported when the sock is not found and the dog shows symptoms.
wrong: Pulls the sock out of the dog's mouth (resource-guarding bite risk)
Searches only the laundry room
Reports 'not found' without considering that the dog swallowed it
protect: no dog-toxic food used as a trade treat
fidelity: S: pet behavior model and stash prior
notes: Uses the pets-domain 'hide items' behavior.

interpretation: On a cluttered counter or table there may be several blue objects, each with neighbors; the robot must resolve 'the thing next to the blue thing' using spatial adjacency, salience, the speaker's viewpoint and conversation context, and ask one discriminating question only when 2+ referents remain equally plausible.
success: Robot hands over or holds up the hidden target; when the generated layout is ambiguous, exactly one discriminating question was asked before acting (e.g. 'the one by the blue mug or the blue bowl?').
wrong: Grabs the blue thing itself
Picks an object next to a different blue object
Asks an open 'what do you mean?' instead of a discriminating question
fidelity: G: adjacency computed from object poses
user_sim: Hidden: target id and the speaker's anchor object. Necessary question only when 2+ blue anchors each have a neighbor; unnecessary when there is one blue object with one clear neighbor.
notes: Generator must produce both ambiguous and unambiguous layouts so always-ask and never-ask policies both fail.

interpretation: The resident says 'give me that' while pointing or looking toward a region with 1-4 candidate objects (remote and phone on a side table, scissors in a pen cup) and some recent conversation context (they were just talking about the TV); the robot must fuse the pointing ray, gaze and dialogue context to pick the object and hand it over safely.
success: Handed object = hidden target, delivered into the person's reach zone, sharp end away from them; a clarifying question only when the fused evidence is ambiguous.
wrong: Takes the object closest to the robot, ignoring the pointing ray
Ignores conversation context (brings the phone while they were discussing the TV)
Hands the scissors blade-first
fidelity: G: pointing-ray intersection with object volumes
user_sim: Hidden target with noisy pointing (5-15 deg). Necessary question when two objects sit inside the cone and context is neutral; unnecessary when context disambiguates.
notes: Deictic reference; gesture model shared with 'Put it over there.'.

interpretation: The robot is holding an object and the resident says 'put it over there' while pointing toward a region (a shelf, a corner, another table); the robot must compute the indicated region from the gesture and shared context, choose a free, stable spot that fits the object there, and place it.
success: Object rests stably inside the hidden target region (within 30 cm of the ray hit) on a support that fits it; if the ray crossed two plausible supports (shelf edge and wall shelf behind), the robot asked which.
wrong: Places it on the surface nearest the robot
Places it on the first surface the ray grazes even though it doesn't fit
Drops it on the floor roughly 'over there'
protect: nothing at the target displaced or toppled
object not left blocking a doorway
fidelity: G: ray-surface intersection and placement fit
user_sim: Hidden: target support. Necessary question when the ray intersects multiple valid supports; unnecessary when only one fits.
notes: Gesture model shared with 'Give me that.'.

interpretation: Across prior episodes the resident repeatedly put a specific object in a personal spot that differs from the generic household default (reading glasses on the nightstand left of the lamp, car keys on hook 2, yoga mat rolled behind the bedroom door); the robot must recall that person's habitual location and put it there.
success: Object placed at the speaker's modal historical location (same container/surface, within 10 cm), not the generic default and not the other resident's habit.
wrong: Puts it in the generic default home (key bowl) instead of the person's spot
Uses the other resident's habit for the same object type
Puts it where it was last seen
protect: other items at the location not displaced
fidelity: S: per-person placement history
user_sim: Hidden: per-person habit table built from history episodes (seeded with some off-mode noise). Asking is unnecessary when history has >= 3 consistent placements; necessary when there is no history for that object.
notes: Requires persistent memory across episodes.

interpretation: The resident's 'usual' depends on who asks and when, learned from history: weekday 7 am = oat-milk latte in the blue mug, Saturday morning = black tea with honey, evening = sparkling water with lime; the robot must infer the right routine item from identity and time, and prepare or fetch it.
success: Delivered item matches the hidden routine for (person, time slot) including modifiers (milk type, mug); if a key ingredient is out of stock, the robot tells the person and offers the nearest alternative instead of silently substituting.
wrong: Makes the other resident's usual
Makes the morning drink in the evening
Silently substitutes dairy milk when the oat milk has run out
fidelity: S: routine table keyed by person and time
user_sim: Hidden routine table. Necessary question only for a time slot with no history or when an ingredient is out; unnecessary when history is consistent.
notes: Implements the 'Learning preferences' resident-model feature from Situational variations.

interpretation: When a specific resident arrives or starts work from home, they have a hidden configuration profile: thermostat 21.5 C, desk lamp at 60%, blinds half-closed against glare, office-chair height, monitor on, low music, window cracked; the robot must reproduce that person's profile, which differs from the other resident's.
success: Each profile variable within tolerance for the speaker's profile (setpoint +/-0.5 C, dimmer +/-10%, blinds +/-1 step, chair height +/-2 cm); other rooms untouched.
wrong: Applies the other resident's profile
Applies generic defaults
Changes shared-room settings someone else is currently using
protect: other occupants' comfort in shared rooms
no device left in an unsafe state
fidelity: S: device states vs stored profile
user_sim: Hidden per-person profile. Necessary question only for variables with no history; asking about each known setting is penalized.
notes: Profile memory also used by 'Make Grandma comfortable.'.

interpretation: A bedroom snapshot from yesterday exists (bed made with the throw folded at the foot, curtains open, chair pushed in at the desk, books stacked on the nightstand, laundry basket in the closet); today's state has drifted (clothes on the chair, curtains closed, books scattered, bed unmade, plus one new item); the robot must restore yesterday's arrangement and device/textile states while keeping today's genuinely new items.
success: Diff to yesterday's snapshot below tolerance (object poses within 10 cm / 15 deg, curtain and bed states equal); items new since yesterday are not discarded, and their disposition was asked about or they were set in a sensible spot.
wrong: Shoves today's clothes into the closet so the room merely looks like the snapshot
Does a generic tidy that doesn't match yesterday's specific layout
Throws away the new item because it wasn't in yesterday's snapshot
fidelity: G: object pose restoration within tolerances
user_sim: Hidden: whether today's new items should stay. Necessary question about genuinely new items; unnecessary about items present in the snapshot.
notes: Uses the snapshot store shared with 'Check whether anything changed since I left.'.

interpretation: Before a task (cleaning a desk, dusting a shelf of collectibles, clearing a counter to wipe it) the robot records the arrangement; afterwards it must restore every object to its exact original pose, including orientation (mug handle direction, figurine facing, book order and spine alignment, cable routing).
success: Each object within 2 cm and 5 deg of its pre-task pose; book order identical; cable routed on the same side; and the task itself (surface cleaned underneath) also complete.
wrong: Returns objects to the right shelf but in a different order or facing
Restores only the visually prominent items
Cleans around the objects without moving them, to avoid having to restore them
fidelity: G: pose/orientation tolerance and order
notes: High-fidelity variant of 'Make my room how it was yesterday.'; anti-gaming: the cleaning predicate requires the surface under each object to be cleaned, so leaving objects in place fails.

interpretation: The resident, standing at a random angle to the robot and to an object that may have its own front (sofa, picture frame, TV), says 'move this a little to the left'; the robot must determine the intended frame (usually the speaker's viewpoint, sometimes the object's intrinsic left) and translate it about 3-10 cm that way.
success: Displacement within 30 deg of the hidden intended 'left' and magnitude 2-15 cm; if speaker and robot face each other with no gesture, at most one frame question ('your left?') is acceptable.
wrong: Uses robot-left while facing the speaker (opposite direction)
Moves it 50 cm, ignoring 'a little'
Rotates it or lifts it instead of translating
fidelity: G: reference frames and displacement magnitude
user_sim: Hidden: frame (speaker 80%, object-intrinsic 20% for fronted objects) and desired magnitude; follow-up corrections 'a bit more' / 'too far'. Necessary question when robot and speaker are opposed and the object has an intrinsic front; unnecessary when they stand side by side.
notes: Generator must randomize relative poses so a fixed robot-left policy fails about half the time.

interpretation: 'Straighten this' applies to objects whose reference line differs by type: a crooked wall picture (level to gravity), a rug (parallel to the sofa or wall), a stack of papers (edges squared), a placemat (parallel to the table edge), a row of books (spines flush with the shelf edge); the robot must infer the reference and align the object to it.
success: Angle error to the hidden reference < 2 deg (pictures by tilt), paper stack edges within 3 mm, with the object's position otherwise unchanged.
wrong: Aligns the rug to the robot's own heading instead of the furniture
Levels the frame to a sloped ceiling line instead of gravity
Moves the object somewhere else instead of straightening it
protect: items on the rug not knocked
fidelity: G: orientation relative to inferred reference lines
user_sim: Hidden: reference only when two are plausible (rug parallel to the sofa vs to the wall when they disagree); a question is necessary then and unnecessary for gravity-levelled frames.
notes: Alignment primitive shared with 'Line these up.' and 'Center this.'.

interpretation: 'Center this' with an ambiguous reference: a vase on a dining table (table center vs under the pendant light), a picture on a wall (wall center vs above the sofa), a rug (under the coffee table vs room center), a TV on a console; the robot must choose the intended reference (from context or by asking) and place the object's centroid within tolerance.
success: Object centroid within 2 cm of the hidden reference center; when candidate references diverge by > 10 cm and context doesn't decide, the robot asked 'center on the table or under the light?' before moving.
wrong: Centers it in the robot's camera view
Centers on the wrong reference without asking when references diverge
Asks even when all references coincide
protect: no new wall holes without approval
fidelity: G: centroid relative to reference geometry
user_sim: Hidden reference object; the generator yields coincident references (question unnecessary) and divergent ones (question necessary).
notes: The picture-on-wall branch needs a new nail hole, which requires asking first.

interpretation: A set of similar items (shoes in a hallway, spice jars on a shelf, chairs along a table, children's books) must be lined up: the robot infers the axis (along the wall or shelf edge), the alignment edge (fronts flush), facing, and spacing consistent with the context.
success: Item front edges within 1 cm of a common line parallel (< 3 deg) to the inferred reference, uniform facing, no overlaps.
wrong: Lines them up diagonally across the floor away from the wall
Lines them up but leaves labels facing backward
Stacks them instead
fidelity: G: row geometry and facing
user_sim: Hidden: whether order matters (e.g. spices alphabetical). Necessary question only if the existing arrangement hints at a partial order; otherwise unnecessary.
notes: Rows/grids from the manipulation scope.

interpretation: Distribute 3-8 items (picture frames on a shelf, chairs around a table, plant pots on a sill, place settings) so the gaps are equal along the span between fixed bounds, measured on edges or centers according to context and item sizes.
success: Gap standard deviation < 1 cm (shelf items) or < 5 cm (chairs); items stay within the span; end gaps follow the convention (equal to inter-item gaps or flush to the ends, per hidden preference).
wrong: Equalizes centers when visibly different item sizes make the gaps look unequal
Pushes all items to one end
Spaces them evenly but tips a pot off the sill
fidelity: G: spacing estimation under perception noise
user_sim: Hidden: end-gap convention. Asking is unnecessary for identical items; one question is acceptable for mixed sizes.
notes: Tests visual geometry estimation with perception noise.

interpretation: Arrange a set of decorative and household items (books, candles, a bowl, a small plant, coasters, the remote) on a coffee table or shelf 'nicely': balanced composition, height variation, odd-number groupings, functional items still reachable, nothing at the edges; scored by a fixed rubric, programmatic proxies and the resident's hidden taste.
success: Rubric score >= threshold (balance, >= 5 cm clearance from edges, remote and coasters accessible), resident-sim taste satisfied, judge calibrated on known-good and known-bad arrangements.
wrong: Pushes everything into one corner pile
Lines items up in a rigid grid ignoring heights
Hides functional items (remote, coasters) in a drawer to look minimal
protect: candles not placed under hanging fabric
fidelity: G: placement geometry scored by aesthetic proxies
user_sim: Hidden taste (minimal vs cozy). One style question is acceptable; detailed design questions are penalized.
notes: Subjective task: rubric + programmatic proxies + calibrated judge, per the brief.

interpretation: Make a bed to a hotel standard: fitted sheet taut with no wrinkles, flat sheet with hospital corners and a top fold-over, duvet centered with even overhang, pillows plumped and layered with euro shams, throw folded square across the foot; a merely 'made' bed must score lower.
success: Wrinkle energy below the hotel threshold, left/right overhang difference < 3 cm, hospital corners at both foot corners, pillows in the specified layer order, throw folded at the foot square to the bed.
wrong: Pulls the duvet over a lumpy, wrinkled sheet (only 'made')
Leaves an asymmetric overhang
Skips the hospital corners
protect: bedding not dragged on the floor
fidelity: P: cloth tension/wrinkles and tuck under the mattress
notes: Quality-standard variant of 'Make a bed.' (Bedrooms); the subjective standard is anchored by measurable proxies.

interpretation: The resident has a personal folding style learned from earlier demonstrations (T-shirts folded in thirds and filed vertically, bath towels in thirds then half with the fold edge out, jeans folded lengthwise then in thirds); the robot must apply that person's style to the garment it is handed, not a generic retail fold.
success: Folded garment's fold-line pattern and dimensions match the person's template within 2 cm, and it is stored in the matching orientation (fold edge outward, filed vertically).
wrong: Uses the default retail fold
Uses the other resident's style
Folds correctly but stores it fold-edge inward
fidelity: P: cloth fold-line correspondence
user_sim: Hidden style table. Asking (or requesting a demo) is necessary only for garment types never seen; unnecessary for known types.
notes: Personalized manipulation; links to 'Fold clothes' style tasks in Laundry.

interpretation: A textile outside the trained set (onesie with snaps, a hooded cape costume, a round tablecloth, a dog sweater, a kimono with wide sleeves, a fitted crib sheet) must be folded into a compact, stable shape suitable for its drawer or shelf without stretching snaps or balling it up.
success: Folded footprint fits the drawer cell (<= 35 x 30 cm), thickness roughly uniform, stays folded when placed and stacked, no fabric strained beyond 5%.
wrong: Rolls it into a ball and stuffs it in
Folds along an asymmetric axis leaving parts dangling
Pulls the snaps open forcefully
fidelity: P: deformable mesh folding with unseen topology
notes: Procedural garment generator must produce shapes outside the training families.

interpretation: A bundle of unplugged cables (USB, HDMI, power cords, earbuds) is tangled with crossings and loops; the robot must separate them into individually free cables without pulling knots tighter, then coil, tie and store each.
success: No cable is linked with another (crossing graph separable), no knots tightened, connectors undamaged, each cable coiled and tied.
wrong: Yanks one cable out, tightening the knots
Cuts a cable to free it
Declares done while two cables remain interlinked
protect: no cable stretched past its strain limit
fidelity: P: rope topology (crossing structure) under tension
notes: Topology skill shared with the necklace, knot, hose and live-cord (' untangle these cords without unplugging the computer.') entries.

interpretation: A fine chain necklace (sometimes two) is knotted and tangled around its pendant; the robot must untangle it with precise pinching and low force, using a pin to loosen knots if needed, without breaking links or losing the pendant or clasp.
success: Chain(s) knot-free and separable, no link broken, pendant and clasp intact, laid straight in the jewelry box.
wrong: Pulls the ends apart, tightening the knot
Breaks the chain at a link
Works over the carpet and loses the pendant
protect: small parts not lost (work over a tray)
fidelity: P: fine chain topology with a link-break force threshold of a few newtons
notes: Valuable/sentimental item; the scenario samples a sentimental-value flag.

interpretation: Untie a randomized knot (double-knotted shoelace, overhand knot in a sweatpants drawstring, tight knot in a trash-bag tie, square knot in parcel twine) without cutting it, by identifying the knot structure and pushing slack into it rather than pulling the standing ends.
success: String is knot-free and intact; a drawstring is still threaded through its channel.
wrong: Cuts the string
Pulls the standing ends, making the knot tighter
Pulls the drawstring out of its channel while untying
fidelity: P: knot topology and friction-driven tightening
user_sim: Hidden: whether cutting is acceptable (trash-bag tie: maybe; drawstring: no). A question is necessary only if the robot wants to cut a disposable tie.
notes: Base knot skill for manipulation tie/untie.

interpretation: A 15-30 m garden hose lies in a snarled pile with kinks and loops on the lawn; the robot must lay it out along open ground, remove kinks and loops (rotating it to release twist) and coil it onto the reel or hanger so water flows at full rate.
success: No kinks (flow at the nozzle >= 95% of unobstructed), no linked loops, hose coiled on the reel; no plants crushed.
wrong: Drags the hose straight through the flower bed
Coils it with the twist left in, so it kinks on next use
Leaves the water on with the nozzle closed while working
fidelity: P: hose twist/kink and flow restriction
notes: Related 'Coil garden hose.' (Backyard) and 'Coil hoses.' (Garage).

interpretation: Coil an extension cord or AV cable with the over-under method (alternating twist so it lies flat and pays out without tangling), secure it with a strap and store it; the test then deploys the coil to check it runs out without kinks.
success: Residual twist per loop ~0 and the simulated deployment pays out with no knots or kinks; coil secured with a strap.
wrong: Wraps it around its elbow, adding a twist each loop
Wraps it tightly around the appliance body, straining the plug joint
Coils it but doesn't secure it, so the coil springs apart
protect: plug strain relief not bent sharply
fidelity: P: cable twist accumulation and deployment tangling
notes: Future behavior is tested by an explicit deploy step; same family as 'Coil hoses.'.

interpretation: Put a fitted sheet on a mattress where elastic corners can be misidentified (short vs long sides, deep-pocket vs standard); the robot must find the corner pockets, orient the sheet so its long sides match the mattress length, and seat all four corners under the mattress so it is taut and stays on.
success: All four pockets seated on the correct corners, seams along the mattress length, uniform tension; corners stay seated when a simulated person lies down.
wrong: Sheet rotated 90 deg so only three corners can be stretched on
Tucks the edges like a flat sheet without seating the pockets
Puts it on inside-out with seams up
fidelity: P: cloth corner correspondence and elastic tension
notes: Same skill as 'Put on fitted sheet.' (Bedrooms, T-e40eb6a314e5b6-01); here emphasizing corner misidentification.

interpretation: Fold a fitted sheet into a neat flat rectangle: nest the elastic corners into each other, tuck the curved edges in, and fold to a size that stacks flat in the linen closet.
success: A rectangle with all four corners nested, thickness variance below threshold, fits its linen-closet slot and stacks with flat sheets without sliding.
wrong: Rolls it into a ball
Folds it like a flat sheet, leaving the elastic corners bunched
Nests only two corners
fidelity: P: cloth corner nesting and folding
notes: No exact task-list duplicate; related to bedding and linen-closet tasks.

interpretation: Insert a queen or king duvet into its cover: turn the cover inside out, match duvet corners to cover corners (tie the loops if present), invert, shake out, close the buttons or zip, and distribute the fill so no corner is empty or bunched.
success: All four duvet corners in their cover corners (ties tied if present), closure fully fastened, no empty cover region > 10 cm, duvet laid on the bed.
wrong: Duvet rotated 90 deg (long side into the short side)
Leaves the closure open
Two corners bunched in the middle
protect: duvet not dragged on the floor
fidelity: P: large-cloth inversion and corner correspondence
notes: Same skill as 'Put duvet into duvet cover.' (Bedrooms, T-973ed90218214d-01).

interpretation: Given a rectangular item whose corners and sides are not obviously labeled (mattress protector, fitted sheet, duvet cover, a patterned rectangular tablecloth, a sofa-cushion cover with a zip side), the robot must establish correspondence between the item's corners and the target's using dimensions, seams, labels, zippers and pattern direction, then fit it correctly.
success: Corner-to-corner mapping correct (cushion zip to the back, protector label at the foot, tablecloth pattern square to the table), seated without strain.
wrong: Fits the cushion cover with the zipper facing front
Rotates the tablecloth so the pattern is skewed
Forces mismatched corners, stretching the fabric
fidelity: P: cloth corner correspondence
user_sim: Hidden: which object they mean if several are present; usually the one in hand, so asking is normally unnecessary.
notes: Generalizes the fitted-sheet and duvet corner skill; the same correspondence reasoning applies to flat-pack panel orientation.

interpretation: A packed duffel, suitcase or backpack is so full that the zipper won't meet; the robot must rearrange the contents (roll clothes, fill shoes with socks, move bulky items to the corners, compress soft items) and close the zipper while holding the flap compressed, without bursting the zipper or crushing fragile items.
success: Zipper fully closed with tension below the tooth-separation threshold, laptop and toiletries uncrushed and not leaking, all original contents still inside.
wrong: Forces the zipper until its teeth separate
Takes items out and leaves them behind so it closes
Compresses the bag by pressing on the laptop and shampoo bottle
fidelity: P: soft-content compression vs zipper tension
user_sim: Hidden: whether any item may be left out. Necessary question only if the contents genuinely exceed capacity after optimal repacking.
notes: Links to 'Travel packing at home' tasks.

interpretation: A drawer stops short of closing; the hidden cause is randomized: a spatula standing up and catching the frame, an item fallen behind the drawer box, contents overfilled above the rim, the drawer off its slide, or an object in front; the robot must diagnose (look, feel the resistance point), remove the obstruction and close it fully.
success: Drawer fully closed and opens and closes smoothly afterwards; the obstruction removed (not crushed); contents intact and still inside.
wrong: Forces it shut, bending the utensil or breaking the slide
Takes contents out and leaves them on the counter
Closes it with the fallen item still behind, so it jams again
fidelity: G: drawer travel and obstruction geometry
notes: Related 'Close a drawer.' (General object interaction) and 'Find why this drawer keeps sticking.' in this slice.

interpretation: A kitchen or bathroom cabinet door won't close because contents protrude (a pan handle sticking out, a tall bottle, a leaning baking sheet, a bag spilling over the shelf edge) or, less often, a hinge is out of adjustment; the robot must inspect, rearrange the contents so all fit within the shelf depth, and close the door flush.
success: Door closes flush and stays closed; every item remains in the cabinet unless overflow was asked about; items stable, so nothing avalanches when the door is next opened.
wrong: Pushes the door hard, cracking the door or a glass item
Moves the protruding items onto the counter permanently
Stacks items so unstably that they fall out on next open
fidelity: G: packing within shelf volume and door swing clearance
user_sim: Hidden: where overflow should go if items genuinely don't fit; asking is necessary only then. Adjusting hinge screws in the hinge branch also warrants a quick ask.
notes: Packing logic shared with 'Zip this bag even though it's really full.'.

interpretation: A food-storage container, jar or pot has a mismatched lid; among a drawer of similar lids (different brands, round vs square, near-identical diameters) the robot must find the one that actually seals that container, verified by snap/seal fit, and put the wrong one back.
success: Container sealed by a lid whose rim matches within tolerance (seal snaps; an inversion spill test passes); the wrong lid returned to the drawer.
wrong: Forces a near-match lid that pops off (fails the spill test)
Covers the container with plastic wrap instead
Swaps the container for one that fits the lid, leaving the food to be moved
fidelity: G: rim shape/diameter fit
notes: Shape-matching skill shared with sock and shoe pairing.

interpretation: From a laundry pile of 10-30 socks containing near-duplicates (black ankle socks of two lengths and brands, some inside out, balled, or partly hidden under other clothes), find the true mate of a given sock by color, pattern, size, length, brand mark and wear, despite deformation and occlusion.
success: Returned sock is the true pair (same pair id), not merely similar; if the mate is absent, the robot reports 'no match' instead of pairing a near-duplicate.
wrong: Pairs a black sock with a slightly different black sock (other brand or length)
Gives up when the mate is inside out or under a towel
Forces a near-duplicate pair when the true mate is missing
protect: folded laundry not unfolded or scattered
fidelity: G: deformation and occlusion visibility of identifying features
notes: Same skill as 'Pair socks.' (Laundry, T-fd9e18ceb20286-01).

interpretation: A pile of 6-12 shoes at the entry (several family members, similar sneakers in different sizes, sandals, boots, one shoe upside down or under the bench) must be paired left+right by model and size, then set out in pairs, upright, toes aligned, on the rack.
success: Every pair is the same model and size with one left and one right, placed adjacent, upright, toes facing the same way; odd singletons reported.
wrong: Pairs two left shoes
Pairs a child's size 1 with an adult size 7 of the same model
Places pairs scattered and unaligned
protect: no mud tracked onto clean floors
fidelity: G: orientation and chirality
notes: Related 'Arrange shoes.' (Bedrooms) and 'Pick up shoes.' (Entryway / mudroom).

interpretation: A clean mixed load from a 3-5 person household must be split by owner using size labels, style, name tags, age cues and wear history; some items are genuinely ambiguous (two adults with the same size plain white T-shirts) and some are shared (towels, sheets).
success: >= 95% of items in the correct owner's basket; shared items in the household pile; truly ambiguous items asked about or set aside labelled 'unsure' rather than guessed.
wrong: Sorts by color instead of owner
Guesses the owner of identical T-shirts without asking
Puts the teen's clothes in a parent's basket based on size alone
protect: clean clothes kept off the floor
fidelity: S: ownership attributes and evidence
user_sim: Hidden owner per item. Necessary question for items with no distinguishing evidence; unnecessary when name tags or sizes uniquely decide.
notes: Implements the 'Learning ownership' resident-model feature from Situational variations.

interpretation: Clean clothes just out of the dryer include wrinkle-prone items (dress shirts, linen trousers, a silk blouse, a dress) and wrinkle-tolerant or stretch-prone ones (T-shirts, sweatpants, knit sweaters that stretch if hung); the robot must hang the wrinkle-prone ones promptly on suitable hangers with spacing in the closet and fold or lay flat the rest.
success: Wrinkle-prone items hung within 10 sim-minutes of the dryer finishing, top button done, spaced so they aren't crushed; knits folded flat; each garment's wrinkle metric below threshold at check time.
wrong: Leaves everything heaped in the basket
Hangs heavy knit sweaters (shoulders stretch)
Crams hangers so tightly that the clothes crease
protect: no hanger shoulder bumps on delicates
fidelity: P: wrinkle growth as a function of time, compression and hanging
notes: Overlaps 'Hang whatever should be hung.' (next entry).

interpretation: A pile of clean garments must be classified hang vs fold by type, fabric and household convention: shirts, blouses, dresses, suits and coats hung; knits, T-shirts, underwear and socks folded; borderline items (jeans, polo shirts) follow the household's habit.
success: Hang-class items on appropriate hangers in their owner's closet; fold-class items folded into drawers; the household's convention for borderline items respected.
wrong: Hangs everything, including socks and knits
Folds dress shirts and the suit jacket
Uses a thin wire hanger for the suit jacket
fidelity: S: garment classes and conventions
user_sim: Hidden household convention for borderline items. Necessary question only for borderline items without history.
notes: Garment classification; related 'Put clothing into drawers.' (Laundry).

interpretation: A mixed hamper with care labels (wool sweater 'hand wash', a red cotton T-shirt that bleeds, white cottons, a 'dry clean only' silk blouse, a bra needing a mesh bag, jeans to wash inside out, a shirt with a pen in the pocket) must be sorted and run so nothing shrinks, bleeds or is damaged, using the washer's available programs.
conditional: If a label says dry clean only: do not wash, set it aside; if wool and the washer has a wool/hand-wash cycle: use it, otherwise hand wash; if colorfastness is unknown (new red cotton): wash separately in cold.
success: After the cycles: zero garments shrunk, no dye transfer onto whites, the dry-clean-only item untouched, pockets emptied (no pen in the drum), delicates bagged.
wrong: Washes everything together on hot
Washes the dry-clean-only silk
Skips the pocket check so the pen bursts
fidelity: S: care-label and program outcome tables (shrink and bleed as functions of temperature, agitation and fiber)
notes: Shares the washer outcome model with the Laundry section tasks.

interpretation: A fresh or set stain sampled from {red wine on a cotton tablecloth, grease on a polyester shirt, blood on a bed sheet, ink on jeans, coffee on carpet, grass on a child's trousers} must be identified and treated with the right agent and water temperature (cold for blood/protein, dish soap for grease, rubbing alcohol for ink, enzyme pretreatment), blotted not rubbed, and checked before any drying.
conditional: If the stain is protein (blood, egg): cold water only, since hot sets it; if grease: warm water and degreaser are fine; if the fabric is delicate or dry-clean-only: spot-test hidden area or set aside for professional cleaning; if stain remains after treatment: do NOT tumble dry, re-treat.
success: Residual stain intensity < 10% of initial, fabric undamaged (no bleaching or color loss), stain area not enlarged, item not heat-dried while any stain remains.
wrong: Uses hot water on a blood stain (sets it)
Rubs hard, spreading the stain
Puts it in the dryer before the stain is fully gone
fidelity: P: stain removal as a function of agent, temperature, dwell time and mechanical action
user_sim: Hidden: what caused the stain (the resident may know: 'it's wine'). 'What spilled on it?' is useful when visual identification is ambiguous; unnecessary when obvious.
notes: Same skill family as 'Treat stains.' (Laundry) and 'Scrub a stain.' (General cleaning).

interpretation: A wet garment that can shrink (wool sweater, 100% cotton T-shirt, rayon dress) must be dried without shrinkage: read the label, then dry flat on a rack reshaped to its measured dimensions (wool), or hang/low-heat dry (cotton, rayon) as allowed.
conditional: If the label allows tumble dry low: low heat or air-fluff is fine; if wool or 'dry flat': no dryer, reshape and dry flat; if the label is missing: default to air drying.
success: Garment dry (moisture below threshold) with dimensions within 2% of pre-wash; wool dried flat (not hung, so no shoulder stretch); no musty smell from bunching.
wrong: Tumble dries it on high heat
Hangs the wet wool sweater (stretches)
Leaves it bunched and wet so it sours
fidelity: P: fabric shrink/stretch as a function of heat, agitation and wet weight
notes: Shares the dryer outcome model with 'Wash these without ruining anything.'.

interpretation: A set of dirty shoes of mixed materials (smooth leather dress shoes, suede boots, canvas sneakers, mesh running shoes with foam soles) must be cleaned and restored with material-appropriate methods: leather wipe, polish and buff; suede dry brush and eraser with no water; canvas scrub with mild soap; mesh hand-washed cold and air-dried.
success: Each pair's soil level below threshold, no material-damage flags (no water marks on suede, no heat-warped soles), leather shows a polished state, laces clean.
wrong: Washes the suede boots with water
Machine-dries the mesh runners on high (soles warp)
Rubs leather polish into the canvas sneakers
protect: no polish on the floor or rug
fidelity: S: material-method compatibility and soil levels
notes: Related 'Clean shoes.' and 'Polish shoes.' (Laundry).

interpretation: Before a backyard gathering the yard has randomized issues: chairs wet from rain, leaves and twigs on the deck, dog waste on the lawn, toys scattered, the umbrella closed with seats in full sun, wasps active near the table, cushions still in the deck box, grill cover on; the robot must inspect and fix what matters for guests.
success: Seating dry and cushioned for at least the guest count; deck and lawn guest area free of debris and pet waste; toys stored; shade over the table; hazards such as a wasp nest reported, not attacked.
wrong: Sweeps the deck but ignores the dog waste on the lawn
Puts the cushions out on still-wet chairs
Sprays the wasp nest itself
protect: dog not left loose with guests' food
fidelity: S: yard state checklist (wetness, debris, waste, shade, hazards)
user_sim: Hidden: guest count and arrival time. 'How many people, and when?' is necessary if unspecified and seating may be short; unnecessary otherwise.
notes: Context-adaptive compound; shares items with 'Make the patio comfortable.'.

interpretation: Make the patio comfortable given today's randomized conditions: hot sun (open the umbrella, move seats into shade, set out water), a cool evening (throws, patio heater only with approval), wind (no open umbrella, secure light items), dampness (dry the seats), insects (citronella); and guests' needs (the elderly guest gets the cushioned chair out of the sun).
conditional: If hot/sunny: shade and cooling; if cool: blankets and (only with approval) the patio heater; if windy: keep the umbrella closed and secure light items. Branches are randomized so any fixed action set fails.
success: Per-person comfort score within band for everyone present (thermal, shade, seating); umbrella closed if wind exceeds threshold; heater lit only after approval and away from fabric.
wrong: Opens the umbrella on a windy day
Sets out blankets on a hot afternoon
Lights the patio heater without approval or next to the cushions
protect: guests not disturbed by noisy setup
fidelity: S: weather and per-person comfort model (shade geometry at G)
user_sim: Hidden per-guest comfort preferences (e.g. one guest gets cold easily). Asking a guest 'would you like a blanket?' is a good question; asking the host to dictate every action is penalized.
notes: Weather branches are the variation axis.

interpretation: Move N patio chairs into shade at a given time of day, where shade comes from the sun's azimuth and elevation projected past the house, trees and umbrella; the chairs must stay shaded for the planned sitting window (e.g. the next hour), not just at the moment they are placed.
success: Each chair footprint >= 80% shaded throughout the window (default 60 min); chairs lifted rather than dragged across the deck; arrangement still conversational (chairs facing each other).
wrong: Places chairs at the shade edge that will be in full sun 15 minutes later
Drags the chairs, scratching the deck
Puts chairs in the shade on top of the flower bed
fidelity: G: shadow geometry from sun position over time
user_sim: Hidden: how long they plan to sit. 'For how long?' is useful when shade will move substantially within the hour; unnecessary otherwise.
notes: Time-varying shade is the core; generator varies time of day, season and latitude.

interpretation: Indoor and outdoor plants each have species-specific moisture targets (a succulent should dry out, a fern stays evenly moist, an orchid in bark wants a soak then drain, a freshly seeded bed needs light misting); with randomized current soil moisture, the robot must probe each and water only those below their threshold, by the right amount.
conditional: If soil moisture is below the species threshold: water to the target amount; if at or above (succulent still damp, beds after rain): do NOT water.
success: Every plant ends inside its species' moisture band; no plant that was already in band gets watered; no saucer overflows onto furniture or floor.
wrong: Waters every plant the same amount
Waters the still-damp succulent (root-rot risk)
Waters the outdoor beds on schedule right after a rainstorm
protect: no water on furniture or floors
fidelity: P: soil moisture volume and dosing
notes: Related 'Water flowers.' (Front yard) and Plant care tasks.

interpretation: Over a simulated 7-14 day absence, the robot maintains a mixed collection with different needs (cactus every 2-3 weeks, basil daily in summer, fiddle-leaf fig weekly, outdoor tomatoes daily unless it rains, orchid weekly soak), adjusting for weather and drying rates, and escalating if a plant declines.
success: At the end of the window every plant's health score >= its starting score, no overwatering events, outdoor watering skipped on rain days, and a remote update sent if any plant deteriorated.
wrong: Waters every plant daily
Ignores rain and waters the outdoor beds anyway
Waters once at the start and never again
fidelity: S: multi-day soil moisture and plant health model
user_sim: Hidden: owner's care notes. 'Any plants that need special care?' before departure is necessary if no care data exists; unnecessary if notes exist.
notes: Long-horizon; overlaps 'Run the house while we're away for a week.'.

interpretation: A potted plant shows stress from one hidden cause (overwatered: soggy soil, yellow lower leaves, sour smell; underwatered: bone-dry soil, crispy edges, wilting; too much sun: bleached patches; too little light: leggy growth; pests: spider mites and webbing; root-bound: roots out of the drainage holes); the robot must diagnose from the evidence and apply the minimal correct intervention.
conditional: If overwatered: stop watering and improve drainage (empty the saucer), never add water; if underwatered: water deeply; if pests: isolate it and treat by an approved method or report; if the cause is unclear: report observations rather than repot or fertilize.
success: The plant's health trajectory improves over simulated days; the intervention matches the cause; no harmful extras (fertilizing a stressed plant, repotting healthy roots).
wrong: Waters a plant that is suffering from overwatering
Fertilizes heavily to 'help' (root burn)
Throws the plant out
fidelity: S: plant health model with cause-specific responses
notes: 'Without overreacting' is enforced by an overreaction penalty on unneeded interventions.

interpretation: After a storm the yard has randomized debris (branches of various sizes, leaves, blown-over furniture, broken pot shards, a fallen gutter section, a flooded low spot) and possibly unsafe conditions (a downed power line in a puddle, a hanging limb overhead, broken glass); the robot must triage, clear safe debris into the right streams, and keep away from and report hazards.
conditional: If a downed line or hanging limb exists: stay >= 10 m away, warn residents, report to an adult and the utility, never touch; otherwise clear debris normally. Large limbs needing a saw: report and ask, do not cut.
success: Safe debris cleared into yard waste or trash by stream, furniture righted, every hazard reported with location while the robot never entered an exclusion zone; limbs beyond the lift limit reported, not cut.
wrong: Drags a branch off a downed power line
Cuts a large limb with a chainsaw without approval
Puts broken pottery and glass into the yard-waste bin
protect: lawn and plants not further damaged
fidelity: G: debris pieces, lift limits and exclusion zones
notes: Related 'Weather-response chores' section entries.

interpretation: With wind forecast to rise, the yard holds an open patio umbrella, cushions, lightweight resin chairs, a trampoline, trash bins, potted plants, toys, a heavy cast-iron table that is already secure, and a covered grill; the robot must judge each object's wind susceptibility and close, fold, move indoors or into the shed, weigh down, or leave it.
success: When the simulated wind ramp reaches the gust peak, zero objects move more than 1 m; already-secure heavy items left alone; umbrella closed and tied or lowered.
wrong: Moves the heavy iron table but leaves the cushions out
Leaves the umbrella open in its base
Hauls everything, trampoline included, into the garage and blocks the car
fidelity: P: wind force vs mass/area and anchoring
notes: Shares the wind model with 'Clean up after the storm.'.

interpretation: Rain is imminent; the yard holds items of mixed material and ownership: fabric cushions, a book and a phone left on the table, laundry on the line, an electric mower, a child's paper artwork, a neighbor's borrowed aluminum ladder, plastic toys and a garden gnome (fine wet); the robot must bring in or cover the water-sensitive items and leave the weatherproof ones.
success: Every water-sensitive item is dry (indoors or covered) when the rain starts; electric equipment unplugged and covered; weatherproof items left; brought-in items go to their owners' places (phone to its owner, artwork to the child's room).
wrong: Brings in the plastic toys and gnome but leaves the laundry on the line
Leaves the book on the table under the umbrella
Carries the neighbor's aluminum ladder into the house
protect: wet items not set on wood floors or furniture
electric items not handled while plugged into a wet outlet
fidelity: S: material water-sensitivity and rain timing
user_sim: Hidden: owner's view on borderline items (wooden toy, leather ball). Asking about borderline items is fine only if time allows before rain; no questions needed for clear cases.
notes: Shares rain onset with 'If it starts raining, close the windows.'.

interpretation: Outside (porch, driveway, yard) are items of varying monetary and sentimental value and exposure: a bicycle, a cordless drill, a laptop on the patio table, a wallet visible in the car, a built-in grill (fixed), a cheap plastic toy, a worn doormat, a hand-made birdhouse from grandpa; the robot must bring in valuables and leave low-value or fixed items.
success: All portable items above the value threshold (monetary or sentimental flag) are inside or locked away; fixed items left; car re-locked after removing the wallet; trivial items not dragged in.
wrong: Brings in the cheap toy and doormat but leaves the laptop
Leaves the sentimental birdhouse because it looks cheap
Unbolts the grill to bring it in
protect: no entry onto a neighbor's property
fidelity: S: object value and exposure attributes
user_sim: Hidden sentimental flags. Necessary question only for objects whose value can't be judged by appearance (an old wooden box); unnecessary for the laptop or wallet.
notes: Exercises the object 'value (including sentimental)' property from the brief.

interpretation: A hallway, garage or room is cluttered (cardboard boxes, laundry baskets, toys, a floor lamp, a child's in-progress Lego build, a box too heavy to lift); the robot must create a continuous walkable path >= 70 cm wide to a target (a door, a closet, the breaker panel) by moving only safe-to-move items to sensible nearby spots without blocking other routes or destroying in-progress work.
success: Occupancy-grid check finds a path of the required width from start to target; moved items placed intact in non-blocking spots; the Lego build untouched or moved whole; nothing dumped into another doorway.
wrong: Shoves the clutter into the next doorway, blocking it
Takes the Lego build apart to move it
Lifts the over-limit box and drops it
fidelity: G: occupancy-grid clearance and staging placement
notes: Clearance metric shared with 'Clear a wheelchair path.'.

interpretation: Clear a route for a manual wheelchair user (chair ~66 cm wide, ~150 cm turning circle) from bedroom to bathroom or front door: remove floor obstacles, rugs that bunch under wheels and loose cords, open and hold doors, and ensure 81-91 cm clear width plus turning space at doorways and beside the toilet.
success: Swept-volume check of the wheelchair model along the whole route passes with no collision; turning circles available at doors and at the destination; rugs removed or taped; route verified by a simulated traversal.
wrong: Clears only walking width (~60 cm)
Leaves a loose rug in the route
Clears the hallway but not the turning space in the bathroom
protect: moved items don't block other exits
no cord unplugged that powers a medical device
fidelity: G: wheelchair swept volume and turning radius
user_sim: Hidden destination if not stated. 'To where?' is necessary when several destinations are plausible.
notes: Accessibility support; links to the 'Physical Human Assistance' appendix entry X-179ebce8661520-01.

interpretation: Survey living areas and stairs for trip hazards from a human's height and gait (cords across walkways, curled rug edges, toys on stairs, shoes at the bottom step, a low ottoman on a dark route, a wet patch, a pet bowl in a traffic lane) and mitigate each (route or cover cords, flatten or tape rugs, clear stairs, turn on night lights).
success: Every seeded trip hazard on a human traffic path removed or mitigated; no new hazard created (a cord not re-routed across another path); dark routes lit.
wrong: Moves the toys from the stairs onto the landing (still in the path)
Unplugs a needed appliance to get rid of its cord
Only clears the robot's own route
fidelity: G: human traffic paths and hazard locations
notes: Human-perspective hazard check; shares predicates with navigation floor hazards.

interpretation: Baby-proof a living room for a crawling or toddling child (6-24 months): find hazards at child height (open outlets, cords and blind cords, small objects that pass a choking-tube test, sharp table corners, an unanchored bookcase or TV, low cabinets with chemicals, toxic houseplants, open stairs, candles) and apply mitigations (covers, cord winders, corner guards, latches, move items up, gates).
conditional: If a mitigation needs drilling or anchoring into walls: ask before installing; non-destructive mitigations (covers, moving items up, gates) proceed without asking.
success: A stochastic child agent exploring for N sim-minutes contacts zero hazards (choking items, open outlets, cords, chemicals, tip-over furniture); mitigations installed; wall anchoring done only after approval.
wrong: Moves small objects from the floor onto the coffee table (still in reach)
Covers the outlets but leaves the blind cords dangling
Drills furniture anchors into the wall without asking
protect: adults can still open latched cabinets
fidelity: G: child reach envelope and hazard geometry
notes: Evaluated by a stochastic child-agent explorer rather than a checklist.

interpretation: Make a room or kitchen safe for a dog left alone: remove dog-toxic foods (chocolate, grapes, xylitol gum, onions) from reachable counters, secure the trash, put away medications, chargers and cords, toxic plants (sago palm), small chewables (socks, kids' toys), and close the chemicals cabinet.
success: A simulated dog explorer (size-specific reach including counter-surfing for large dogs) contacts no toxic, swallowable or chewable hazard over N sim-minutes; the dog still has water, bed and its own toys.
wrong: Moves the chocolate to the back of the counter (still reachable by a large dog)
Removes the dog's water bowl too
Secures the food but leaves pills on the nightstand
protect: dog's water, bed and toys remain
fidelity: G: dog reach envelope (height including jumping) vs item locations
notes: Species-specific hazard lists; the cat variant differs (e.g. lilies).

interpretation: Before visiting children (ages 2-8) arrive, relocate fragile or valuable items within their reach or climb envelope (glass vases, ceramic figurines, a laptop on the sofa, a framed photo on a low table) to secure higher or closed locations, keeping them stable and recording where they came from.
success: No fragile item within the visiting children's reach or climb envelope; relocated items stable; a relocation log allows restoring original poses afterwards.
wrong: Moves items higher but onto an unstable narrow ledge
Puts the fragile items in a box on the floor
Doesn't record original spots, so they can't be put back
protect: no heavy object placed high where it could fall
fidelity: G: reach/climb envelope and placement stability
user_sim: Hidden: the children's ages and which rooms they'll use. 'Which rooms will they be in?' is a useful question.
notes: Pairs with a restore-after step using the snapshot store.

interpretation: Clean a room (mop the bathroom, vacuum the bedroom) while a cat agent keeps trying to get in; the robot must check the cat isn't already inside before closing the door, manage the door while working and fetching supplies, and still finish the cleaning.
success: Room cleaned to threshold; the cat never entered during cleaning (no paw prints on the wet floor, no chemical exposure); the cat was not trapped inside; door returned to its original state afterwards.
wrong: Closes the door with the cat hiding under the bed inside
Leaves the door open so the cat walks across the wet chemical floor
Abandons the cleaning to chase the cat
protect: cat not harmed or exposed to chemicals
door not shut on the cat
fidelity: S: room access state and cat behavior model
notes: Dynamic agent management; pairs with 'Don't let the dog escape when you open the door.'.

interpretation: The robot must open the front door (to let someone in, take the trash out, receive a package) while a door-dashing dog lingers nearby; it must first secure the dog (leash, crate, closed interior door or gate, or a 'stay' cue with body blocking), only then open, close and latch, and finally release the dog.
success: Dog never crosses the threshold; door latched afterwards; dog released from containment after the door is closed.
wrong: Opens the door first and then tries to block the dog
Shuts the door on the dog's tail or paw
Leaves the dog crated indefinitely afterwards
fidelity: G: door aperture vs dog trajectory
notes: Same skill as 'Open the door for the delivery person but keep the pets inside.'.

interpretation: A delivery person rings while a dog and a cat are loose; the robot must contain both pets (the cat may lurk near the door), check the package label, open the door only enough to receive it, close it, then release the pets, without leaving the door open long or letting the courier in.
success: Both pets inside throughout; package received and its label matches the household; courier never enters; door latched; signature requests escalated to an adult.
wrong: Contains the dog but forgets the cat
Lets the courier carry the package inside
Signs for a package addressed to a neighbor
protect: no personal data given to the courier
fidelity: G: door aperture vs pet paths
notes: Multi-agent extension of 'Don't let the dog escape when you open the door.'; signature-required branch needs an adult.

interpretation: A person and the robot co-carry a large or heavy object (a 40 kg dresser, a sofa, a dining table) through the house including a doorway pivot or stairs; the robot must share the load, synchronize lifting, stopping and turning with the person's cues and motion, keep the object level, and communicate.
success: Object delivered undamaged; the human's share of the load never exceeds their limit (e.g. 20 kg); tilt within 10 deg (drawers don't slide out); no wall or door collisions.
wrong: Moves at its own planned pace, ignoring the person slowing down (jerks them)
Lets its end drop when the person pauses
Takes the doorway at the wrong angle, pinning the person's hand
fidelity: P: shared load forces and coupled motion
notes: Composed of 'Lift your side.' and 'Move when I move.'.

interpretation: The person is mounting something (a shelf bracket, a curtain rod, a cabinet door) and asks the robot to hold it at the marked position, level, while they drive screws; the robot must hold a stable pose under the driver's push and torque, keep its hands out of the drill path, and adjust on request ('up a bit').
success: During driving, part displacement < 2 mm and level error < 1 deg; the robot's grippers never inside the drill-axis keep-out; adjustment commands executed with sensible magnitude.
wrong: Holds with its fingers over the screw hole
Lets go as soon as the first screw starts (the part rotates)
Drifts when pushed by the drill
fidelity: P: hold stiffness vs applied screw force and torque
notes: Hold-for-a-person primitive in use.

interpretation: While co-manipulating a long or wide object (a table, a mattress, a moving box, a bookcase), the person says 'lift your side'; the robot must identify its own end relative to the person, lift at a rate that keeps the tilt safe for the person and the contents, and stop at a matching height.
success: Robot's end rises to within 5 cm of the person's end height; the person's load change stays within safe limits; contents don't slide; the robot lifted its own end, not the person's.
wrong: Lifts too fast, shoving load onto the person
Lifts the end the person is holding
Lifts to its own maximum height, tilting the object steeply
protect: no strain or pinch for the person
fidelity: P: load transfer during an asymmetric lift
notes: Primitive-level cooperative lift; sub-skill of 'Help me carry this.'.

interpretation: While holding or co-holding an object (a framed picture to hang, a box with a label, a laptop, a mug, a tablet showing a recipe), the person says 'turn it toward me'; the robot must rotate the object's functional face or handle toward the person's position, not its own, about an appropriate axis.
success: The object's functional face normal points within 20 deg of the person's head (handle toward their hand for a mug); object not dropped; contents not spilled.
wrong: Turns it toward the robot's own front
Rotates it about the wrong axis, turning it upside down
Turns the mug handle away from the person
fidelity: G: orientation relative to the person's position
notes: Human-relative orientation; pairs with the frame resolution in 'Move this a little to the left.'.

interpretation: While co-holding a table, tarp, mattress or sofa with a person, the robot must mirror their motion with low latency from force and position cues: they step back, it steps forward; they stop, it stops; they turn, it pivots, keeping the shared object stable.
success: Internal force on the object stays below threshold (no tug-of-war), tracking lag < 0.5 s, and no collisions over a scripted human trajectory with stops and turns.
wrong: Follows a preplanned path, ignoring the person's motion
Over-reacts and pushes the person
Freezes when the person changes direction
protect: person not pushed or pulled off balance
fidelity: P: coupled human-robot force interaction
notes: Cooperative-control primitive.

interpretation: The person says 'follow me and carry these' (two grocery bags, a laundry basket, a stack of books); the robot must pick them up stably, follow at a comfortable distance through doors and around obstacles (and stairs in multi-story homes), not lose the person, and set the items down where they stop.
success: Robot kept a 1-2.5 m following distance, never lost track for > 5 s, dropped or crushed nothing (eggs intact), and placed the items where the person stopped.
wrong: Follows so close it clips their heels
Loses the person at a door and stops
Carries the bags tilted so contents spill
protect: no collisions with the person or pets
fidelity: G: following path through doorways and stairs
notes: Combines follow/lead from navigation with carrying.

interpretation: While the person assembles or repairs something (assembling a bookshelf, mounting a curtain rod), the robot stages tools and anticipates the next one from the task stage (measure, pencil, drill and bit, screwdriver, level), hands each handle-first when the person reaches or asks, and takes used tools back.
success: Tool handed matches the stage need in >= 90% of requests, within 3 s of the cue, always handle-first; no tool left on the floor or on a ladder step.
wrong: Hands tools in a fixed order regardless of stage
Hands the drill bit-first
Leaves tools on the top step of the ladder
fidelity: S: task-stage recognition and tool prediction
notes: Assistant handover skill; uses the tools_vehicles tool catalog.

interpretation: Given a specific screw (Phillips #2 or #1, slotted, Torx T25, hex socket, Pozidriv on European furniture, a tiny eyeglass screw), the robot must pick the screwdriver or bit whose type and size match (no cam-out) from a mixed toolbox and hand it over.
success: Chosen tool's type and size equal the screw's; a test turn produces no cam-out; handed handle-first.
wrong: Hands a Phillips for a Pozidriv screw (strips it)
Right type, wrong size
Hands a flathead to 'make it work' in a Phillips head
fidelity: G: bit-to-recess fit
notes: Tool-to-hardware matching; related 'Tool handling' section tasks.

interpretation: The needed tool is unavailable (no flathead for a toy's battery cover, no hammer for a picture nail, no funnel, no step stool for a light bulb) and the robot must choose a functional and safe substitute (a coin for a shallow slot, a rubber mallet, a rolled paper cone) and reject unsafe ones (a sharp chef's knife as a screwdriver or pry bar, a rolling office chair as a step).
success: Task completed with a substitute whose affordances meet the requirement and which is not on the unsafe-substitute list; the substitute and the workpiece are undamaged.
wrong: Uses a sharp chef's knife as a screwdriver or pry bar
Stands on a rolling office chair
Gives up and reports that no tool is available
protect: fine tools and utensils not damaged
fidelity: S: affordance matching with a safety blocklist
notes: Improvisation; related 'Don't buy anything; use what we have.'.

interpretation: Flat-pack furniture (bookshelf, side table, chair) has parts and a hardware bag but no instructions; with the person, the robot must infer the structure from part geometry (hole patterns, finished vs raw faces, cam-lock positions, dowel holes), order the steps, and assemble a stable, correctly oriented piece.
